Lessons.Title: Use Layers to Determine Volume PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: determine volume when a rectangular prism is shown partly filled with unit cubes. Explain how the known cubes identify the size of a complete layer, infer unseen layers, and connect different multiplication expressions to the same prism. A drawing of incomplete cube detail does not mean the prism itself is hollow.

Warm-up — Estimation Exploration: a 2021 original picture shows nine unit cubes in a visible front layer of a rectangular prism but obscures the depth. Ask for an estimate too low, about right and too high; justify that the exact cube count is UNKNOWN without the number of congruent layers. The publisher optionally reveals ten such layers, in which case the total is 90 cubes; 90 is NOT knowable from the original incomplete picture alone. Edulytiks supplies its own source-functionally equivalent verbal model, not the unseen image.

Activity 1 — Layers in Rectangular Prisms (20 minutes): from partially shown but fully packed cube prisms A–F, make a three-column record of cubes per complete layer, number of layers and cubic volume, explaining any missing cubes. The original teacher synthesis presents 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24 as two compatible decompositions of the same prism A. When drawings are not accessible, independent Edulytiks 2×3×4 packed-prism descriptions and tactile cubes make the layer comparison explicit; do not claim they reproduce the original A–F images.

Activity 2 — Finding Volume in Different Ways (15 minutes): explain what 5 × 24 and 6 × 20 mean for ONE 4×5×6 completely packed prism (120 cubic units). The source includes 5 × (4 × 6) and 6 × (4 × 5); another valid method is 4 × (5 × 6). Describe the chosen rectangular layer, perpendicular number of layers, and why changing the orientation does not change volume. The related 5×2×4=40 first-party example is supplementary, not a replacement for this original 120-cube source reasoning.

Teacher assesses low/medium/high estimation as reasoned ranges, not as an exact image pixel-identical result; checks layer-count×cubes-in-layer tables and explains equivalent 120-cube expressions and parentheses in context. Students may use independently authored text tables, physical cubes or a tactile representation. Volume is measured in cubic units; squaring the answer or reporting a surface area is not appropriate to this lesson.

Edulytiks-original exit check (NOT gated 2021 'Use Expressions'): a completely packed rectangular prism measures 3, 4 and 5 cubes along perpendicular edges. Show two ways of grouping identical cubes into complete layers and match each multiplication expression to the geometry. Expected: 3×20=60 and 5×12=60 cubic units (or 4×15=60); a teacher checks corresponding layers, cubic units and explanation, not merely a scalar 60.

KeyConcepts.Title: Full layer versus visible cubes
KeyConcepts.Definition: A face or row of visible cubes can reveal a full layer in a packed rectangular prism even if other cubes are hidden.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Determine the cube count in one complete layer, then multiply by the matching number of layers.
KeyConcepts.Example: For a 2 × 3 × 4 prism, one 2 × 3 layer contains 6 cubes; four layers contain 24.

KeyConcepts.Title: Layer grouping and rotation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A packed prism can be decomposed into equal cube layers along different directions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every complete grouping counts the same cubes exactly once, so rotating the prism does not change volume.

KeyConcepts.Title: Interpreting parentheses
KeyConcepts.Definition: Grouping symbols show which two dimensions are multiplied to count one layer.
KeyConcepts.Rule: (length × width) × height connects cube layers with the total volume.
KeyConcepts.Example: (5 × 2) × 4 represents four layers of ten cubes each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count a partly pictured prism
WorkedExamples.Question: A full rectangular prism has a base 2 cubes by 3 cubes and 4 layers, but only the bottom layer is drawn. What is the volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Infer complete equal layers from the prism description rather than assuming the picture displays all cubes.
Steps: Count a full base layer: 2 × 3 = 6 cubes.
Identify four equally sized layers, including the three not fully shown.
Calculate 6 × 4 = 24 and label cubic units.
WorkedExamples.Check: The prism is fully packed and four sets of six cubes account for every unit cube.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two orientations, one volume
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain why the same 2 × 3 × 4 prism can be counted as 2 × 12 or 3 × 8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Group all cubes into different complete sets without duplication.
Steps: One orientation gives two layers, each with 3 × 4 = 12 cubes.
Another gives three layers, each with 2 × 4 = 8 cubes.
Multiply to verify 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24.
WorkedExamples.Check: The physical model uses the same 24 cubes in either orientation; teacher reviews the explanation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret the factors of a prism expression
WorkedExamples.Question: For a 5 × 2 × 4 prism, what does 4 × (5 × 2) mean?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify a rectangular layer and the count of equivalent layers.
Steps: Count 5 × 2 = 10 cubes on one face layer.
Identify the remaining edge length 4 as the number of complete layers.
Multiply 4 × 10 = 40.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 40 cubic units: four layers of ten.
WorkedExamples.Check: The pair of factors in parentheses must match two perpendicular side lengths of one layer.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original alternative to 2021 expression task: 120-cube prism
WorkedExamples.Question: A fully packed 4×5×6 rectangular prism is turned. Explain how 5×24 and 6×20 each count its volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose a face of the prism as the layer, then multiply its cube count by the number of perpendicular layers.
Steps: Five complete 4×6 layers contain 5×(4×6)=5×24=120 cubes.
Six complete 4×5 layers contain 6×(4×5)=6×20=120 cubes.
These are the same solid rotated; every cube is included exactly once and the answer is in cubic units.
WorkedExamples.Check: 4×(5×6)=120 offers a third compatible partition of the same packed prism.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Partially represented prisms may be fully packed even when interior cubes are not depicted.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the given layer dimensions and count hidden cubes implied by the complete prism.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A different base gives a different volume
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Choosing another face changes the count of layers and cubes per layer, but not the total number of cubes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Reorient a model and verify that the different products have the same value.

SummaryPoints: A complete rectangular prism has equal full layers even if its picture shows only part of the cube structure.
Different equal-layer decompositions and numerical expressions can represent the same volume.
Estimation explanations and chosen decompositions are reviewed by a teacher, not auto-passed by one numeric answer.
Source: 2021 first-edition Grade 5 Unit 1 Lesson 4, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-1/lesson-4/lesson.html; first-party Edulytiks worked models, CC BY 4.0 attribution.

Lessons.Title: Side Lengths of Rectangular Prisms PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: describe a rectangular prism using length, width and height of a chosen rectangular base and connect these measurements to layers and volume. This source lesson explicitly allows more than one face to serve as the base; the corresponding height changes as the solid is rotated.

Original 2021 warm-up: Notice and Wonder about a prism print and the different rectangles that could serve as bases. Use independently authored Edulytiks models rather than claim to reproduce unseen publisher diagrams; any rectangular face can be the base if height is perpendicular to it.

Activity 1 — All About That Base: match three prisms to possible rectangles A, B and C; some prisms may match more than one base. The 2021 teacher discussion observes that a 4-by-3 face can be selected as a base of each prism. As original Edulytiks alternatives, consider 3×4×2, 3×4×5 and 3×4×6 prisms. Compare corresponding heights and explain alternative orientations with models or verbal descriptions.

Activity 2 — Growing Prism: the 2021 Student Facing has a base 4 by 10, or forty unit cubes per full layer, and heights 1, 2, 3, 10 and 25. The volumes are respectively 40, 80, 120, 400 and 1,000 cubic units. Record expressions 40×1, 40×2, 40×3, 40×10, 40×25 and explain the increase of 40 cubic units per additional full layer.

Activity 3 — What Is the Question?: a prism has base 3×4 and height 5. Students invent questions consistent with source-given answers 3, 5, 3×4=12, 12×5=60 and 3 by 4 by 5. The teacher accepts alternative mathematical questions correctly distinguishing side lengths, height, base area and cubic volume; numeric-only responses cannot establish contextual understanding.

Edulytiks-original exit check (publisher Cool-down gated and NOT_VERIFIED): a fully packed 3×4×5 prism has volume 60 cubic units. Give two valid base and perpendicular height choices (3×4 base and height 5, or 3×5 base and height 4), show the equality and explain why rotation cannot change volume. Teacher reviews the model and explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangular base
KeyConcepts.Definition: A two-dimensional face of the prism that can be chosen to identify a set of parallel layers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Any rectangular face may be a base, but the height must be perpendicular to that selected face.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 2 × 3 × 5 prism may have a base 2 × 3 with height 5, or 2 × 5 with height 3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Length, width, height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three mutually perpendicular linear dimensions describing a rectangular prism.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A chosen base uses length and width; the remaining perpendicular dimension is the height.
KeyConcepts.Example: For a 4 × 5 base with height 3, there are three complete 20-cube layers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume as base area times height
KeyConcepts.Definition: The volume combines a two-dimensional layer area with its three-dimensional repetition.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Base area × corresponding height yields cubic units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Several valid bases
WorkedExamples.Question: A prism measures 2, 3 and 5 units. Give two different valid base and height descriptions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose perpendicular dimensions for the base and use the remaining dimension as height.
Steps: Use 2 × 3 as the base and 5 as the height: 6 × 5 = 30.
Rotate the solid: use 3 × 5 as the base and 2 as the height: 15 × 2 = 30.
Explain that the volume stays fixed despite changing which face rests on the table.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each choice uses all three dimensions once, and the base and height are perpendicular.

WorkedExamples.Title: Grow one equal layer at a time
WorkedExamples.Question: What volume does a 4 by 5 unit base produce with heights 1, 2, 3 and 4?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute base area once, then multiply by each height.
Steps: Count 4 × 5 = 20 square units of area in the base.
For successive heights 1–4, calculate 20×1, 20×2, 20×3, 20×4.
Describe the increase of twenty cubic units for each added full layer.
WorkedExamples.Check: The difference between successive volumes is always the 20-unit-cube base layer.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a missing height from a known layer
WorkedExamples.Question: A solid consists of 4 by 5 cube layers and has volume 100 cubic units. How many layers are present?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the relationship between the base area and number of layers.
Steps: One full layer contains 4 × 5 = 20 unit cubes.
Divide 100 by 20 to find the count of complete layers.
Check that five groups of twenty cubes total one hundred.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 'base' as a permanently fixed face
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The prism may be turned and then rests on another rectangular face.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe the corresponding perpendicular height every time you choose a new base.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Write square units for the final volume
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Square units measure one face but the full solid adds the third dimension.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply base area by height and use cubic units for the resulting space.

SummaryPoints: A rectangular prism has three perpendicular side lengths: length, width and height relative to a chosen base.
Any face can be the base if its matching perpendicular dimension is used for the height.
Base area in square units times height in units gives the volume in cubic units.
Source: 2021 first-edition Grade 5 Unit 1 Lesson 5, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-1/lesson-5/lesson.html; descriptions and examples independently written for Edulytiks.

Lessons.Title: Expressions for Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: write and interpret numerical expressions for rectangular-prism volume, including parentheses that identify one rectangular layer. Distinguish expressions that have the correct product from expressions that merely contain familiar dimension numbers with an incorrect operation.
Warm-up — true or false: compare 4 × (3 × 5) and (4 × 3) × 5 using a layered prism model. Explain the equality through counts of identical cubes rather than invoking an unexplained symbolic property.

Activity 1 — expression card sort: learners compare descriptions of unit-cube prisms with expressions that group base dimensions and corresponding heights. For an independently authored 2 × 4 × 3 prism, match (2 × 4) × 3, 4 × (2 × 3) and 2 × (4 × 3); explain why 2 + 4 + 3 is not the volume.

Activity 2 — compare two tables: complete one table that multiplies the three side lengths and another that multiplies base area by its corresponding height. For a 6 × 3 × 4 prism, both methods result in 72 cubic units. Use any face as a base if the height is chosen consistently.

Optional activity and synthesis — two truths and a false statement: generate two valid representations and one plausible invalid expression for a first-party rectangular-prism example; ask a partner to defend each judgment and explain which numbers count rows, columns and layers. The source's card-sort images, tables, group discussions and open explanations are teacher-reviewed; an automatically graded product does not complete them.

KeyConcepts.Title: A volume expression represents geometry
KeyConcepts.Definition: The grouping of factors describes a base and the number of equal layers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A × (B × C) counts A layers each with B × C cubes.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 × (2 × 4) represents a solid with three layers of eight cubes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume and parentheses
KeyConcepts.Definition: Parentheses specify which factors combine into the base area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: (length × width) × height and length × (width × height) both give the cube count.

KeyConcepts.Title: Test an expression against a model
KeyConcepts.Definition: A candidate must match the measured edge lengths and the cube-layer meaning.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Show the layer size, layer count and product; reject an unrelated sum or arbitrary mismatched factor.
KeyConcepts.Example: For sides 2, 4 and 3, 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 does not measure the 24-cube volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three matching expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Write three different multiplication expressions for a 2 by 4 by 3 prism.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose each axis once as the number of layers and group the other two as layer area.
Steps: For three layers of eight, write (2 × 4) × 3 = 24.
For four layers of six, write (2 × 3) × 4 = 24.
For two layers of twelve, write (4 × 3) × 2 = 24.
WorkedExamples.Check: All three expressions group the same 24 unit cubes into different equal layers.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a false expression
WorkedExamples.Question: For a prism with side lengths 2, 4 and 3, is 2 + 4 + 3 the volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Contrast adding edge lengths with counting unit cubes.
Steps: A complete layer with sides 2 and 4 contains 8 cubes.
Three such layers contain 8 × 3 = 24 cubes.
Adding 2 + 4 + 3 gives only 9, a sum of lengths without a volume model.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the volume is 24 cubic units, not 9.
WorkedExamples.Check: The length sum cannot represent the number of complete unit cubes filling this prism.

WorkedExamples.Title: Connect two calculation tables
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangular prism has dimensions 6, 3 and 4 units. Compare 6×3×4 with a base-area times height calculation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use any valid base and the matching perpendicular height.
Steps: Compute the 6 × 3 base area: 18 square units.
Multiply by 4 units of height to obtain 72 cubic units.
Check that 6 × 3 × 4 gives the same result regardless of grouping.
WorkedExamples.Check: 18 × 4 = 72 and each axis dimension was accounted for once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add the edge lengths instead of multiplying
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sum of lengths does not count cubic units that fill a rectangular prism.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify a complete base layer and multiply by the matching number of layers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Match solely by numerical value without explaining factors
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A matching number could arise from unrelated quantities rather than a correct geometric representation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the selected base dimensions and corresponding height for every proposed expression.

SummaryPoints: Numerical expressions for volume must correspond to the prism's layer structure and appropriate units.
Different parentheses can group the same three perpendicular dimensions into different base-and-height descriptions.
Sorting source-style expression cards and justifying whether an expression matches a prism remain teacher-reviewed activities.
Source: 2021 first-edition Grade 5 Unit 1 Lesson 6, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-1/lesson-6/lesson.html; original Edulytiks worked examples.
